headline: Cockenoe on the Flood: Bunker-Fed Blues, Porgies Thick on the Cows
subhead: The reef bite is splitting by tide window this week — blues and bass on the bunker push, sea bass and scup holding tight to structure while the stripers wait on a cool front.
body_markdown:
The call this week is Cockenoe Reef on the incoming, not Penfield. That's the read off the water temp split — Kings Point sitting at 70.9 on the western end of the Sound, New London down to 69.4 to the east. That gradient matters because it tells you the bait and the blues are still riding warm water on our side of the Sound, while any cooling influence is still miles off. Cockenoe sits in that warmer western pocket, and with bunker schools thickening up and down the coast this week, that reef is where the bait is stacking on the flood, and where the bluefish are camped on top of it.

The 44th Annual Surfside Hotel bluefish tournament fleet has been working these waters hard, and the reports back that up — chopper blues from 4 to 8 pounds are hammering peanut bunker pushed up against the rockpiles off Cockenoe and out toward Sheffield Island on the last two hours of the flood, when the current stacks bait against the structure instead of sweeping it past. Diamond jigs, 2 to 3 ounces, tin-side up, worked with a fast erratic retrieve through the froth, are outfishing bucktails right now — the blues want speed, not finesse. Anyone throwing bunker chunks on a fish-finder rig off the stern anchored just up-current of the reef is getting steady action too, though you're picking through smaller blues doing that versus the jig bite on the edges.

Stripers are the trickier read. We flagged this last week — said nighttime striper activity would gradually improve on structure as temps ease, and that's exactly the shape of it right now. Daytime bass are still mostly staged rather than committed, sitting on bait but not blitzing, because 70-plus degree water on our end of the Sound isn't forcing the issue yet. The building moon toward full on the 6th and 7th is going to tighten those bunker schools further, and once a real cool front finally shows up, that's when this turns into the first legitimate fall pattern. Until then, the better bass have been coming after dark off Greenwich Point and along the drop at the western edge of the Norwalk Islands, working bunker spoons and 6-inch swimshads slow along the rock edges on the last of the ebb, when current pulls bait off the structure into the deeper water bass are holding in.

Penfield Reef is still worth the trip, but the tide window there is unforgiving — you want the last two hours of the ebb, when the reef's rockpile sheds current hard enough to concentrate blackfish and porgies but not so hard you're fighting a boat full of Saturday traffic for swing room. Blackfish are just starting to wake up on that structure as the water eases from summer highs — nothing explosive yet, but fish to 4 and 5 pounds are coming off the deeper boulders in 20 to 30 feet on green crab and Asian crab, worked tight to bottom with a light enough sinker to feel the structure change. That bite should build through the month as the water keeps sliding down.

The more consistent structure bite right now is porgies and black sea bass. The Cows off Stamford are holding scup thick in 15 to 25 feet — small hooks, squid strips or sandworms on a simple high-low rig, and you don't need much weight in that lighter current. It's meat-and-potatoes fishing, but it's steady, and it's a good call for anyone trying to avoid the weekend boat parade around the Norwalk Islands, since the Cows see a fraction of the traffic. Black sea bass are holding on the same structure that's been good all summer — the rockier stretches off Cockenoe and the deeper edges around Sheffield Island, 25 to 35 feet, squid and butterfish strips fished on bucktail-and-teaser combos right on bottom. Sizes have been solid, plenty in the 14 to 16 inch range with a few bigger mixed in.

Fluke are on the seasonal slide everyone expects this time of year — the doormat-class fish are pulling out toward deeper ocean-side structure, and what's left inside is thinning fast. Still worth a drift through the channels between the Norwalk Islands on the last of an outgoing tide if fluke is the target, using 4-inch white Gulp on a 3/4-ounce bucktail dragged slow along the sand-to-rock transitions, but don't plan a whole trip around it. That bite's closing, not opening.

Looking ahead, the next few days should hold this same split pattern — bluefish staying aggressive on bunker through Labor Day week as the tournament fleet keeps proving out, porgies and sea bass steady on the same structure that's carried the summer, and stripers building toward something real but not there yet. If the first real cool front of the season lines up with this building moon, expect the switch to flip fast — that's usually how it goes here, bass go from scattered to committed within 48 hours once the trigger hits. Until then, fish the tide windows tight: Cockenoe on the flood for blues, Penfield on the last of the ebb for tog, and the Cows anytime for a guaranteed bend in the rod without fighting for space.
